code_label: CVaR replaces expectation as objective
text_span: we propose the Conditional Value-at-Risk as an aggregation function
rationale: States the paper’s central methodological change to variational optimization.

code_label: Faster convergence and better solutions claimed
text_span: this leads to faster convergence to better solutions for all combinatorial optimization problems tested in our study
rationale: Summarizes the main empirical finding reported in the abstract.

code_label: Analytical explanation provided
text_span: We also provide analytical results to explain the observed difference in performance between different variational algorithms.
rationale: Indicates the paper includes theory to explain performance differences.

code_label: CO problems mapped to Hamiltonians
text_span: There is a well-known transformation to map CO problems into a Hamiltonian
rationale: Describes the standard encoding used to connect combinatorial optimization to quantum algorithms.

code_label: Expectation-based objective used in prior work
text_span: minimize the expectation of the problem Hamiltonian for a parameterized trial quantum state.
rationale: Defines the baseline objective that the paper modifies.

code_label: Sample mean as estimator
text_span: The sample mean (5) is an estimator for ⟨ψ(θ)| H |ψ(θ)⟩
rationale: States how the expectation value is estimated in the standard approach.

code_label: Diagonal Hamiltonians make best sample more relevant
text_span: for problems with a diagonal Hamiltonian, such as CO problems, the sample mean may be a poor choice in practice.
rationale: Motivates why expectation minimization may be misaligned with combinatorial optimization.

code_label: Best observed outcome is practical target
text_span: it is therefore reasonable to focus on improving the properties of the best measurement outcome, rather than the average.
rationale: States the practical objective underlying the CVaR proposal.

code_label: Minimum observed outcome is too non-smooth
text_span: the minimum observed outcome over a set of measurements: min{H1, ..., HK}. However, for finite K this typically leads to a non-smooth, ill-behaved objective function
rationale: Identifies a drawback of using the raw minimum as the objective.

code_label: CVaR smooths tail-focused objective
text_span: To help smooth the objective function, while still focusing on improving the best measured outcomes rather than the average, we propose the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR)
rationale: Explains why CVaR is introduced as the optimization criterion.

code_label: CVaR interpolates between minimum and mean
text_span: the limit α ↘0 corresponds to the minimum, and α = 1 corresponds to the expected value of X.
rationale: Defines the role of α and positions CVaR between two extremes.

code_label: No one-to-one mapping of local minima
text_span: A local minimum of (1) does not necessarily correspond to a local minimum of (13), and vice versa.
rationale: Formal analytical result about the changed optimization landscape.

code_label: Example where expectation is flat
text_span: using (1) yields a constant objective function on which no optimization can be performed.
rationale: Shows a case where the standard expectation objective provides no gradient signal.

code_label: CVaR yields smoother optimizable landscape
text_span: CVaR with 0 < α < 1 yields a smooth objective function that is optimized by decreasing θ.
rationale: States the beneficial effect of CVaR in the illustrative example.

code_label: Sample complexity increases as alpha decreases
text_span: The variance of the empirical CVaRα estimator using K samples is O(1/(Kα2))
rationale: Quantifies the estimation cost of using smaller α values.

code_label: Need more samples for same accuracy
text_span: to achieve the same accuracy as for the expected value we need to increase the number of samples to K/α.
rationale: States the practical sampling overhead implied by CVaR estimation.

code_label: Broad benchmark suite used
text_span: we test the proposed on multiple random instances of six CO problems
rationale: Describes the experimental scope and benchmark diversity.

code_label: Extensive simulation study design
text_span: we run CVaR-VQE and CVaR-QAOA for α ∈{1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%}
rationale: Specifies the parameter sweep used in the experiments.

code_label: COBYLA used for classical optimization
text_span: Following [17], we use the classical optimizer COBYLA to determine the parameters of the trial wave function.
rationale: Identifies the classical optimizer used throughout the study.

code_label: Probability of optimal solution chosen as metric
text_span: We compare the diﬀerent algorithms by plotting the resulting probability of sampling an optimal solution
rationale: States the main evaluation metric used instead of objective value.

code_label: Metric chosen because objectives differ
text_span: comparing algorithms with respect to the average objective function value (or CVaR with a diﬀerent α) would not be informative.
rationale: Explains why the paper uses overlap with the optimum as a common comparison metric.

code_label: Higher depth and lower alpha improve performance
text_span: The plots show that increasing p and decreasing α has a positive impact on the performance.
rationale: Summarizes the main simulation trend across settings.

code_label: CVaR-VQE outperforms expectation baseline
text_span: with p = 2 and α = 1%, within 50 normalized iterations we achieve at least 1% probability of sampling an optimal state for almost all instances.
rationale: Provides a concrete performance result for CVaR-VQE.

code_label: QAOA weaker than VQE at comparable depth
text_span: QAOA’s performance appears signiﬁcantly worse than that of VQE for equivalent depth
rationale: Reports a comparative finding between the two variational families.

code_label: Limited QAOA parameters as explanation
text_span: We conjecture that this is due to the limited number of variational parameters in QAOA: only 2p, compared to n(1 + p) for VQE.
rationale: Offers the authors’ explanation for QAOA’s weaker performance.

code_label: Hardware results show same beneficial effect
text_span: on quantum hardware we observe the same beneﬁcial eﬀect on the speed of convergence that was observed in the noiseless simulation results.
rationale: States that the CVaR advantage persists on real hardware.

code_label: CVaR may ignore low-quality samples
text_span: A possible explanation is that the CVaR objective function allows us to ignore some of the low-quality samples from the quantum state.
rationale: Provides a tentative mechanism for why CVaR helps on noisy devices.

code_label: Noisy CVaR estimate can still help
text_span: even a noisy CVaR esti- mate yields better results than a more accurate expected value estimate.
rationale: Highlights a counterintuitive empirical observation about noisy estimation.

code_label: QAOA can produce flat states
text_span: QAOA may produce relatively “ﬂat” state vectors, i.e., with amplitudes of similar magni- tude.
rationale: States the key analytical behavior investigated for QAOA.

code_label: Flat states limit probability mass concentration
text_span: for ﬁxed p there is the risk that the amplitudes remain ﬂat.
rationale: Identifies a limitation of shallow QAOA circuits.

code_label: Need well-distributed objective values
text_span: QAOA requires the diagonal elements of the Hamiltonian (i.e., objective function values) to be well-distributed to eﬀectively “mix” and increase the amplitudes.
rationale: Explains a condition under which QAOA can improve amplitudes.

code_label: Small depth may miss optimal sampling
text_span: it may not put enough em- phasis on the tail of the distribution of objective function values to sample an optimal or a near-optimal solution.
rationale: Connects flatness to reduced chance of sampling good solutions.

code_label: Hardware noise and decoherence constrain depth
text_span: the current generation of quantum hardware is aﬀected by non-negligible gate errors and decoherence, successfully implement- ing circuits with large depth may be out of reach for the moment.
rationale: States a practical hardware limitation affecting deeper circuits.

code_label: Alpha choice trades off focus and reach
text_span: the CVaR objective function with α = 1% does not reward increasing the overlap with the ground state beyond 1% probability.
rationale: Notes a built-in ceiling effect from very small α values.

code_label: Empirical alpha recommendation
text_span: Results in this paper suggest choosing α ∈[0.1, 0.25] as a good empirical choice
rationale: Provides a practical recommendation derived from experiments.

code_label: Section absent
rationale: All major sections are present in the provided paper text; no absent section code is needed.
